clue.text: Fuss about nothing made when Captain Oates' rum runs out?

indicators.note: whatever runs out scatters in all directions, so the name and the drink leave in a jumbled order

blocks.note: fifteen letters of fodder: the explorer's rank and name plus the drink

explanation.surface: An Antarctic tent where the famous explorer makes a scene because the rum supply has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Oates, of Scott's doomed polar party, famously walked out into a blizzard, so 'runs out' fits the story neatly while signalling the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes great agitation over a trivial matter, which is exactly a fuss over nothing much.

clue.text: Those being treated in hospital where clap set in, unfortunately

indicators.note: something that has gone unfortunately has gone wrong

blocks.note: to clap someone on the back is to give them a pat
the five letters of 'set in' rearranged

explanation.surface: A cheeky hospital scene hinting that a venereal disease has taken root on the ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clap' in the surface suggests the slang for gonorrhoea, but here it is simply a friendly slap, a PAT.
explanation.definitionFit: People receiving medical care on a ward are called by the standard noun for anyone under a doctor's care.

clue.text: Right to run away?

blocks.note: slang for legitimate, above board
British slang for fleeing on foot, using the body part that does the running

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as LEG IT and it becomes British slang for running off at speed; kept whole it is short for legitimate.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal speech clips legitimate to this form, meaning proper, lawful, correct, as in 'the deal is all above board'.

clue.text: Kick outside a match official for wearing no shoes

blocks.note: to boot a ball is to kick it
taken as printed
short for referee

explanation.surface: An angry footballer lashing out at the referee, with a hint that he had taken his boots off.
explanation.walkthrough: The football surface makes 'kick' and 'match official' feel like the story rather than the wordplay, so the solver hunts for a foul, not a word to split.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with bare feet has nothing on them, the plain meaning of going unshod.

clue.text: Patched-up bathroom finally completed

blocks.note: the last letter of 'bathroom'
something completed has ended

explanation.surface: A home renovation report: the bathroom has at last been patched up and finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' seems to belong to 'completed' in the surface, but it works on 'bathroom' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Repaired things have been fixed, so a patched item is one that someone has repaired.

clue.text: Greeting used by members of ethnic group claiming a mountain range

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it

blocks.note: an informal hello
the people of Malaysia and neighbouring lands
taken as printed

explanation.surface: A cultural note about how members of an ethnic group greet each other, drifting into a land dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: The A goes into MALAYS between the Y and the S.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Asian chain containing Everest, the world's highest peaks, so it is a proper example of such a range.

clue.text: Terribly ill outside hospital department? Find pulse!

indicators.note: something done terribly is done badly

blocks.note: the three letters of 'ill' rearranged
Ear, Nose and Throat, a standard hospital unit

explanation.surface: A hospital drama: a very sick patient wheeled outside a ward while someone shouts to check for a pulse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' in the surface is a heartbeat; as the definition it means an edible seed such as a pea or bean.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are the dried edible seeds of legumes, and the small round lentil is a standard example.

clue.text: For a warm layer, choose grandma's second patterned cable knit

indicators.note: a pattern arranges strands in a new design

blocks.note: to elect is to choose, as in a vote
position two of 'grandma'
the nine letters of 'cable knit' rearranged

explanation.surface: Knitting advice: to make something cosy, pick grandma's second cable-knit pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cable' in the surface is a knitting stitch, but it quietly suggests the flex of the answer; 'patterned' is the signal to rearrange it.
explanation.definitionFit: A heated bed covering is spread as a layer on the mattress to keep a sleeper warm.

clue.text: Out-of-condition partner in no-win situation

blocks.note: an athlete who is stale is past peak form
a mate is a partner or companion

explanation.surface: An unfit partner leaves a couple stuck in a situation neither can win.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase about an unfit partner, but it splits into two plain synonyms placed one after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess this is a drawn position where neither player wins, so it names any deadlock generally.

clue.text: Perfect setter to hand out cards?

blocks.note: the setter speaks of themself as I
to deal is to distribute cards to players

explanation.surface: Someone praising a card player as the perfect person to deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' means the crossword's compiler, who refers to themself as I, not a dog or a card-game role.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something flawless, exactly matching every wish or standard.

clue.text: Opening in workplace, when fellow leaves for Rhode Island

indicators.note: one piece goes away and another takes its place

blocks.note: a place of work
F is the abbreviation for fellow, as in FRS
the US state's postal abbreviation

explanation.surface: An office job opening: a colleague departs for a new life in Rhode Island.
explanation.walkthrough: OFFICE has two Fs; swapping either one for RI gives the answer. 'Opening' looks like a vacancy in the surface but is a physical hole.
explanation.definitionFit: An orifice is a hole or aperture, especially in the body, so it is a formal synonym for gap.

clue.text: Unpleasant doctor has a staff shortage

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for doctor
taken as printed
a staff is a stick, cut short by one letter

explanation.surface: A disagreeable GP whose surgery is short of employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees in the surface; in the wordplay it is a walking stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Drastic measures are harsh and severe, so the word carries the sense of hard to bear or disagreeable.

clue.text: Money-making herb?

blocks.note: the verb for stamping coins, and the name of the place that does it
the aromatic garden plant used in sauces and tea

explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen makes it look like one idea, a profitable plant, but the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Mint strikes coins, producing currency; separately, spearmint and peppermint are common garden herbs.

clue.text: Carol singer may be an uninvited visitor

blocks.note: read literally, someone who calls at doors in the chill of December
the usual sense: a salesperson who turns up or phones without an appointment

explanation.surface: A grumble about Christmas singers who knock at the door without being asked.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is usually a sales pitch; the clue reads it literally, as a caller out in winter weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold calling is approaching strangers with no prior contact, so such a person arrives unasked and unexpected.

clue.text: Tried suspect and got together to limit new damage

blocks.note: the five letters of 'tried' rearranged
people who met came together
standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A court case where a suspect is tried and people gang up to contain the fresh harm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tried suspect' looks like a courtroom phrase, but 'suspect' is the instruction working on 'tried'.
explanation.definitionFit: Detriment means harm or loss, as in 'to the detriment of his health', a direct synonym.

clue.text: Beginning of Bonnington's ultimate climb?

indicators.note: 'ultimate' means last, so only the final letter of the climber's name is kept

blocks.note: the last letter of the mountaineer's name
an ascent is a climb up a mountain

explanation.surface: The start of a famous mountaineer's final great expedition.
explanation.walkthrough: Chris Bonington is a celebrated British mountaineer, so 'ultimate climb' reads as his last expedition; 'ultimate' only takes his last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nascent is an adjective for something just coming into existence, as in a nascent industry at its start.

clue.text: Flexible European to remain in charge

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for European
to last is to endure or remain
i/c is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A pliant European politician who wants to stay in power.
explanation.walkthrough: IC for 'in charge' comes from the written abbreviation i/c, as in 'officer i/c'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stretchy that bends and springs back is supple, the physical sense shared by both words.

clue.text: Barge's cargo typically contains a snail

indicators.note: the phrase before holds the answer within it, running across the word breaks

blocks.note: running from the end of the first word through the second into the third

explanation.surface: A canal boat's load is usually said to include a snail, fittingly slow travel.
explanation.walkthrough: It is the French word for a snail, and a barge is a fittingly slow, French-canal image.
explanation.definitionFit: The French culinary name for an edible snail, borrowed into English menus.

clue.text: River found in collapsed coal pit is very hot

blocks.note: the seven letters of 'coal pit' rearranged
standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A mining disaster report: a river breaks into a collapsed pit and the heat is intense.
explanation.walkthrough: The R slips in after the first letter of the rearranged fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Regions near the equator have hot, humid climates, so the word is used for sweltering weather.

clue.text: Time to take old beer back to secure accommodation

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for time
standard abbreviation for old
a brew is beer, as in home brew
to secure a door is to lock it

explanation.surface: Last orders: time to return the stale beer and find somewhere safe to stay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secure accommodation' is a real phrase for a locked facility, which disguises that 'secure' is wordplay and only 'accommodation' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall building of flats is housing where many people live, so it is a kind of residence.

clue.text: Grow as a biennial's pungent root

blocks.note: running from the end of the first word into the start of the fourth

explanation.surface: Gardening advice on a strong-tasting root crop that grows over two years.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate signal here; the gardening surface makes the run of letters look like advice about growing the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese horseradish-like plant has a fiery green rhizome, grated as a condiment with sushi.

clue.text: Youngster embarrassed to turn up for run

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up makes the word read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
someone embarrassed goes red

explanation.surface: A bashful child who is reluctant to show up for a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' is not a race but a line of broken stitches in tights or stockings; British English calls it a ladder.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a snag that unravels a stocking is a ladder, the American word for which is run.

clue.text: Thin metal sword

blocks.note: metal beaten or rolled into a very thin sheet, as used in the kitchen
the light, blunt-tipped blade used in fencing

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one description of a slender blade, which hides the separate kitchen-wrap sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitchen wrap is a thin sheet of aluminium; in fencing, the lightweight practice blade has this name.

clue.text: Bid for treasure chest with missing lid

indicators.note: in a down entry the lid is the top

blocks.note: a coffer is a strongbox for valuables

explanation.surface: An auction lot: a treasure chest whose lid has gone astray is up for sale.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, the lid of the word is its top letter, so the C goes.
explanation.definitionFit: At an auction a bid is an amount a buyer proposes to pay, a price put forward.

clue.text: Adopted animal and bird from east for daughter

indicators.note: reading from the east in an across entry means going right to left

blocks.note: a donkey
the flightless Australian bird
standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A family adopts a pet animal and a bird brought from the East for their daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For daughter' simply adds D at the end. 'Adopted' reads as taking in a pet, but defines as taking on, as in an assumed name.
explanation.definitionFit: An adopted name or manner is taken on as your own, the same sense as in 'an assumed identity'.

clue.text: Funfair disrupted by thug

indicators.note: a disrupted event is thrown into disorder, and so are the fair's letters

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A fairground day ruined by a violent troublemaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disrupted by thug' reads as one news phrase, but 'by' only joins the rearranged fair to its definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent, lawless person or bully is called by either word; they are close synonyms.

clue.text: City-bred Dutch expelled from South African port

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for Dutch
the port city on South Africa's east coast

explanation.surface: Townsfolk of Dutch descent being thrown out of a South African harbour city.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes South Africa's Dutch settlers, making 'Dutch' look like part of the history rather than a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone raised in a town has a metropolitan upbringing, and the adjective describes things of towns.

clue.text: Acquit former partner facing single charge

indicators.note: to face something is to stand in front of it

blocks.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner
one is single
a charge or fee is a rate

explanation.surface: A court clears someone's ex who faced just one count.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' suggests a criminal count in the legal surface, but here it is a price.
explanation.definitionFit: To exonerate is to declare someone free of blame, which is what a court does when it finds them not guilty.
